doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Deciding to become a writer and magazine work
summary: After the Army he decided to be a writer, struggled, then wrote for all the major magazines.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: Day jobs: musicians working outside music

blocks.x: Well I think it’s got to have great importance that you did that and that you’re still doing it and that you were inspired to write about jazz.

Well yes you know as I say I didn’t know what I was going to do when I got out of college but then by the time I realized I was going to get out of the Army I knew I had to make up my mind and I just sort of said well I guess you’re going to be a writer. That was sort of like it seemed fated. Nothing ever occurred to me that I ought to do anything
else. And I didn’t look forward to it with great glee. I wasn’t saying oh boy I’m going to be the next Proust or something of that kind, because I’d seen too much of it.
You didn’t have any like pie in the sky ideas.
No, I knew what it was and while I wanted, like all of my people of my generation, you all wanted to be Ernest Hemingway, you know, chicks, the Riviera—

Right. Great business. But so I set out to be a writer and I’ve never looked back and I’ve never felt sorry and I struggled like anyone else beginning to get published, and eventually I did get published and then I began writing for the magazines and to make — I had a wife and children and all the rest of the nonsense that goes along with twenty-first century America. And I had — to make a living I was writing for the magazines. By the time I’d been doing for, I don’t know four or five years, five or six years, I was writing for all the top magazines, the big six women’s magazines: Redbook, Cosmopolitan, Vanity — not Vanity Fair, Glamour, Esquire, The New Republic, Sports Illustrated, Reader’s Digest, Playboy, Penthouse, all of them.
